source.title: Tight Bounds for Logistic Regression with Large Stepsize Gradient Descent in Low Dimension

record.file_problem: none; the complete paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Reports results for large-step gradient descent on separable logistic regression, a linear-model setting outside the neural-network claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own convergence bounds and numerical results for logistic regression. These do not test the neural-network, initialization, width, normalization, or squared-loss conditions named in the versions.
record.test_reason: The study proves convergence bounds and reports experiments for separable linear logistic regression. These results do not test V5's neural-network recovery, curvature reduction, stability-threshold hovering, or divergence claims. The other versions concern architectures and training comparisons absent here. Related edge-of-stability findings are discussed as motivation.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: sufficiently large constant stepsizes yield a stepsize-independent stable-transition bound for two-dimensional separable logistic regression, with a worst-case lower bound matching up to logarithmic factors. Higher-dimensional numerical evidence motivates a conjecture, not a proved extension.
record.recipe_differences: Full-batch GD on convex linear logistic regression with a zero initialization and large constant stepsizes; the claim versions concern neural-network training and other specific recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The stepsize is a central varied setting in the MNIST experiment and random search; the paper reports that increasing it creates instability and faster optimization, while the observed transition time does not increase. The proved upper bound applies only for d = 2 and η above the stated threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: For two-dimensional separable logistic regression, sufficiently large constant stepsizes give transition time O(n/γ + log(1/γ)/γ²), independently of η, followed by loss at most 8/(ηγ²(t−τ)). Constructed datasets give a matching lower bound up to logarithmic factors.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Large-step GD on separable linear logistic regression in two dimensions reaches monotonic convergence within a stepsize-independent transition bound that is tight up to logarithmic factors.

fits_no_version.finding: On a binarized MNIST subset of 256 examples, larger constant stepsizes produce instability and faster optimization without an apparent increase in transition time.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Across the tested constant stepsizes, logistic-regression transition time on this MNIST subset does not increase.

fits_no_version.finding: Random searches with n=d and dimensions 2 through 128 find maximum transition times that do not exceed about 60 as stepsizes increase; the search is not exhaustive.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sampled higher-dimensional separable logistic-regression problems exhibit bounded transition times across the tested large stepsizes.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, vol. 336; 39th Annual Conference on Learning Theory (2026)
record.problems: The proved upper bound is restricted to d = 2. Higher-dimensional evidence is a non-exhaustive random search. The MNIST and higher-dimensional numerical results are presented in figures without precise values in the text.

untested.parts: Convolutional-network training error, CIFAR-10/100, random or corrupted labels, and model-size or regularization comparisons.
Spurious minima and extra student neurons in two-layer ReLU teacher-student networks.
Depth-related training degradation, identity shortcuts, and deep-network initialization or normalization alternatives.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, orthogonal weights, training speed, and trainable depth.

Wide-network squared-loss recovery above the initial linearized stability limit, curvature reduction, divergence at larger rates, sharpness hovering at the stability threshold, and divergence from below that threshold.
Batch-normalization speed and learning-rate tolerance comparisons, including Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: States are assessed against the supplied versions. Assigning cannot_determine to these unlinked rows does not question the paper's logistic-regression results.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses linear logistic regression, not convolutional networks; it does not test random initialization, CIFAR benchmarks, corrupted labels, or model size.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student problem or width comparison.
No deep plain or residual neural networks, shortcuts, or normalization comparison.
No neural-network initialization or depth comparison.
The study examines large stepsizes for logistic loss, not the stated wide-network squared-loss setting, stability limit, or sharpness dynamics.

rows.subject: Gradient Descent (GD) for Equation (1)
rows.size_stated: linear model in d = 2; dataset size n
rows.operation_detail: Full-batch gradient descent with constant stepsize on separable logistic loss; initialization w0 = 0.
rows.measure: Stable transition time τ to F(wt) ≤ 1/8η, then logistic loss
rows.value: τ ≤ 2 + 4n/γ + 280 log(2/γ²)/γ²; for t > τ, F(wt) ≤ 2/(ηγ²(t − τ))
rows.locator: Theorem 2.1; Lemma 2.8; Appendix A, Theorem 2.1 proof
rows.note: The paper also states the asymptotic transition bound τ ≤ O(n log(1/γ)/γ + 1/γ²). This is a bound for convex linear logistic regression, not a result on the neural networks in the claim versions.
rows.check: The result concerns linear logistic regression, so it cannot establish any listed version. The explicit post-transition bound in Appendix A, Equation 155, is 8/(ηγ²(t−τ)), not 2/(ηγ²(t−τ)). The asymptotic transition bound is O(n/γ + log(1/γ)/γ²), correcting the note's placement of the logarithmic factor.

rows.subject: Gradient Descent (GD) for Equation (1)
rows.size_stated: linear model in d = 2; dataset size n
rows.operation_detail: Full-batch gradient descent with constant stepsize on constructed separable logistic-loss datasets; initialization w0 = 0.
rows.measure: Stable transition time τ to F(wt) ≤ 1/8η
rows.value: There exists a dataset with τ ≥ Ω(n/γ + 1/γ²).
rows.note: Worst-case lower bound over constructed datasets; the theorem does not claim that typical datasets stall.
rows.check: The worst-case lower bound concerns constructed linear logistic-regression datasets and cannot establish any listed version. Its stated value and conditions match Theorem 3.1.

rows.subject: GD on a subset of MNIST
rows.operation_detail: Gradient descent on logistic loss with exponentially increasing stepsizes.
rows.measure: Stable transition time and optimization loss
rows.note: The text describes larger learning rates as creating instability and faster optimization, and says the stable transition time does not increase; precise plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: This linear logistic-regression experiment cannot establish any listed version. Figure 1(a) compares runs at exponentially spaced constant stepsizes; it does not describe a stepsize increasing exponentially within each run. The experimental transition criterion is F(wt) ≤ 2/η.

rows.subject: GD on randomly generated datasets
rows.operation_detail: Numerical search over datasets to measure the maximum time to reach F(wt) ≤ 2/η.
rows.measure: Maximum stable transition time τ across searched datasets
rows.value: Figure-only; text says the worst-case τ does not increase past 60 as η increases exponentially.
rows.note: The authors qualify this as numerical evidence from a random search that is not exhaustive.
rows.check: The sampled linear logistic-regression results cannot establish any listed version; 'partial' is therefore inappropriate. Section 4 generates 4096 datasets for each dimension–stepsize pair, rather than merely for each dimension. The reported maximum remains at most about 60; this is evidence within the sampled search.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
